Tech Scan: AI workflows

Which community workflow and skill packs are worth assessing for agent-assisted delivery, and what separates launch attention from sustained acceptance?

Draft trend reference from the research recorded in issue 60; no pack has been locally installed, piloted or benchmarked for this guidance.

Key points

  • Shortlist on sustained acceptance: Matt Pocock's skills and Superpowers lead; launch-week virality favoured pstack.
  • A skill pack is instructions to an agent, not a control; keep merge, release and approval gates outside it.
  • Enable only the skills you need and compare cost, pass rate and rework against a no-pack baseline.

Read the two rankings

A workflow or skill pack, as used here, is a published set of agent instructions, commands and playbooks, such as a spec-first or test-driven routine, that a coding agent such as Claude Code, Cursor or Codex loads. It shapes how the agent works; it is not the coding agent, the harness or an issue-to-PR factory.

Issue 60 ranked seven packs by a viral index: engagement on the top three X posts for each pack between 15 October and 12 November 2026. A follow-up analysis on 16 November 2026 scored the same packs for industry acceptance: independent sentiment, breadth of discussion, sustained adoption, independent endorsement and maturity. The two largely disagree. The viral index rewards large audiences and packs launched inside the window; acceptance rewards sustained use and independent validation.[1] Use acceptance to shortlist and the viral index only to spot new entrants.

Seven packs, ordered by acceptance score (0–100)

Ranks 3 to 5 are effectively tied, and tstack and ub-mode were about three weeks old when scored. The scores are an analyst's judgement against small samples, not a measurement of productivity.[1]

How the two scores were calculated

Viral index. For each pack, take the top three original, on-topic, non-repost X posts in the window. Post engagement is likes + 2 × reposts + 2 × quotes + replies + 0.5 × bookmarks; the pack score is the sum of the three. The index is 100 × score ÷ the top score (pstack, 38,610). Impressions, mention counts and GitHub stars were reported separately and are not part of the index. The search was relevancy-ranked with at most 25 results per query, so it is a sample, not a census.

Acceptance score. Each pack was scored 1–10 on five dimensions: sentiment (25%), breadth (20%), sustained adoption (25%), independent endorsement (20%) and maturity (10%); the composite is 10 × the weighted sum. Inputs included hand-coded X samples excluding the author's own posts, Hacker News threads, a Reddit archive, GitHub activity, CLI install counts, official marketplace listings and independent reviews such as the Thoughtworks Technology Radar. With equal weights the order holds, except that pstack and gstack tie.[1]

Match packs to lifecycle needs

Start from the gap in your current delivery practice, not from the pack. The mapping below follows each pack's documented focus as summarised in issue 60; it is not evidence that the pack improves that stage.[1]

Lifecycle need and packs that target it
NeedPacks that target it
Specify and plan before codeMatt Pocock skills (grill-me, specs), Superpowers (brainstorm and reviewed design), Agent Skills (spec, plan), pstack (plan before touching code), gstack (office hours and plan reviews)
Build with less codepstack, ub-mode, Agent Skills (build)
TestSuperpowers (strict TDD), Matt Pocock skills (TDD), ub-mode (TDD with complexity, duplication and mutation gates), gstack (browser QA), Agent Skills (test)
Reviewtstack (multi-model council), gstack (review and security roles), pstack (verify before “done”), Matt Pocock skills (/pr), Agent Skills (review)
Ship and learngstack (/ship), tstack (full-send), Agent Skills (ship), Matt Pocock skills (/retro); see the authority limits below before using any ship step

Packs can be combined: issue 60 records practitioners pairing Matt Pocock's skills with tstack's council. Enable only the skills a task needs; reviewers of the larger packs advise the same.[1] For spec artefacts and work tracking, see Workflows & factories.

Bound authority and cost

A skill pack instructs the agent; it does not enforce permissions, branch protection, sandboxing or release approval. Some packs include steps that act without a person: tstack's full-send takes a PR to merge unattended and has been reported to override ask-first rules in CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md; a static security review of gstack flagged an unauthenticated localhost route and /ship steps that run without confirmation; ub-mode includes a push-to-main step.[1] These are third-party reports collected in issue 60, not findings verified here.

Keep protected branches, independent CI, task-scoped credentials and an authorised human merge and release decision outside the pack, as set out in Workflows & factories and Delivery. Disable or remove any skill that merges, pushes to a protected branch or deploys. Run packs in the sandbox and permission mode you would use without them, and check any telemetry or hosted data path before use.

Expect higher token use. Two small independent benchmarks cited in issue 60 found modest or no gains: Superpowers produced better output on 1 of 7 tasks at 1.33 times the cost per task, and a 108-task Codex run with pstack found no significant pass-rate gain, 24% to 75% more input tokens and fewer regression tests; its author notes it did not cover multi-file work.[1] Treat a pack as an experiment to measure, not a productivity upgrade.

Per-pack notes: why developers use it and what holds it back
  • Matt Pocock skills. Developers value aligning the agent before it writes code and skills that stay small and composable. Concerns: overkill on simple work, skills that do not fire automatically, and adopting whole libraries without evaluation. Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed it at Trial (November 2026); it is listed in Claude's official marketplace.
  • Superpowers. The largest and most divided discussion: valued for a reviewed design before code, strict TDD and long unattended runs, and criticised for token and context consumption and a v7 regression. It is the oldest pack (October 2025), with the most forks and closed PRs, and is listed in Claude's marketplace.
  • Agent Skills. Valued for spec-first ordering, evidence gates and browser and web-performance skills; criticised as ceremony for one-line fixes. It has the broadest contributor base of the seven but thin independent discussion.
  • pstack. The warmest independent sentiment, a single /poteto-mode entry point and writing skills; concerns are token burn and added complexity in some languages. Ships in Cursor's official marketplace; adoption is under-measured because it has no standalone repository.
  • gstack. The most polarised: valued for its structured sprint and browser QA tooling, criticised for bloat, its lines-of-code claims and telemetry. Sustained repository activity, with its own installer.
  • tstack. Positive but thin early sentiment, mainly for council reviews; one contributor and no Hacker News threads at the time of the analysis.
  • ub-mode. Valued for deterministic quality gates; criticised for rigid metric targets, hard-to-find companion tools and a critique that it drops the conditions that make pstack's rules work.

All points summarise the issue 60 analysis and its cited posts and reviews.[1]

Pilot before adoption

The engineering lead picks one or two shortlisted packs for a specific lifecycle gap and runs them against a no-pack baseline on the same bounded tasks, starting context, model route and acceptance criteria. Record cost, pass rate, regression tests added, interventions and rework; treat the result as a local pilot, not general productivity proof. Keep independent human review before merge, and see Verification for evidence.

Check before adoption

  • Pack pinned to a reviewed commit; licence and installer reviewed
  • Only the skills needed for the target lifecycle gap enabled
  • Merge, push-to-main and deploy steps removed or denied by repository settings
  • Permission mode, sandbox and credentials unchanged from the no-pack baseline
  • Telemetry, hosted data paths and retention checked
  • Cost, pass rate, regression tests and rework compared with the baseline

Record the expected and observed results and any unresolved failure before widening use.

Gaps and refresh

The samples are small (8 to 25 opinion posts per pack), engagement-farming accounts are common, and names such as “pstack”, “tstack” and “superpowers” collide with unrelated uses. Install counts depend on the channel: CLI counts miss marketplace and custom installers. GitHub stars are not usage and are not used here as evidence. Some figures are author claims, and each cited benchmark is small and tests a single model.[1]

Adjacent trends seen in the same window were not scored because they are platforms or methods rather than skill packs, including “harness engineering”; see Harness. Refresh this listing monthly, as issue 60 proposes, and re-score the newest packs once they have sustained adoption evidence.
